items.title: Robert Kabera, Rwandan Government Critic, Beheaded in Uganda
items.summary: The former soldier had been living in exile since 2020, and said in a video posted this month on TikTok that he feared for his life.
items.full_text:
Title: Robert Kabera, Rwandan Government Critic, Beheaded in Uganda - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/world/africa/rwandan-beheaded-uganda-kabera.html

Published Time: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 22:23:06 GMT

Markdown Content:
A vocal critic of Rwanda’s government who fled to Uganda in fear of his life has been found beheaded, the police say.

The authorities launched an investigation after the body of Robert Kabera, a former Rwandan soldier, was found Saturday in a district 30 miles southwest of the capital, Kampala, a police spokesman, Rusoke Kituuma, said on Monday.

The head was still missing, he said.

Mr. Kabera, 50, had used social media to attack Rwanda’s president, Paul Kagame. In one video posted this month on TikTok, he said he feared for his life. “Kill us if you want,” the video was titled, pledging that “Major Robert will say the truth.”

Human rights groups say that Mr. Kabera’s death fits a pattern in which people regarded as opponents of Mr. Kagame have been assassinated abroad, sometimes in gruesome fashion. A spokeswoman for Rwanda’s government, Yolande Makolo, did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday.

Nearly a dozen high-profile Rwandan dissidents have been targeted or killed after fleeing the country, [according to](https://www.hrw.org/report/2023/10/10/join-us-or-die/rwandas-extraterritorial-repression#:~:text=attacks.%5B169%5D-,Killings,-Since%20the%20RPF) rights groups. They include former military personnel, opposition figures and journalists.

The deaths undercut Rwanda’s image as a nation that restored itself after the genocide of 1994. Rwanda, a country of just 15 million, punches far above its weight in financial terms, and has risen to become one of Africa’s most prominent economies.

Its latest public relations coup was the announcement this month of a 10-year deal to host the [Formula 1 African Grand Prix](https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/article/formula-1-returns-to-africa-with-10-year-agreement-to-race-in-rwanda.13xs9VMK7cGFiBd2IplyES) in Kigali.

“Under President Paul Kagame, political dissent in Rwanda carries serious risks, and documented efforts to silence critics have extended beyond the country’s borders,” an opposition group in exile, the Rwanda National Congress, said in a statement about Mr. Kabera’s death.

Human rights groups have documented “a pattern” of transnational assassinations by the Rwandan authorities, said Lane Hartill, a researcher at Amnesty International. “Rwanda doesn’t accept internal dissent, particularly from former members of the military and ruling party,” he said.

The Rwandan authorities have disputed those accusations, saying that Rwanda is setting its own course toward political and economic development, one that emphasizes national unity.

But threats to stability are often dealt with swiftly.

Mr. Kabera fled Rwanda in November 2020. Days later, the authorities said they were investigating him for, they claimed, sexually assaulting a relative. The Ugandan authorities granted him asylum as well as security protection, though in 2022 Rwanda’s government asked Uganda to extradite all Rwandan citizens it considered a threat. The two countries have close security ties.

On two occasions, Mr. Kabera was beaten while he lived in hiding, according to Human Rights Watch. The group said in a 2023 report that they feared for Mr. Kabera’s safety, in part given the close security ties between Rwanda and Uganda.

Two of the most high-profile killings of Rwandan dissidents took place in South Africa.

In 2021, one opposition figure, Seif Bamporiki, was [shot dead](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/22/world/africa/rwanda-seif-bamporiki-killing.html) in Cape Town after he delivered a bed from his store to a client. The authorities in South Africa said that the motive seemed to have been robbery, but his friends said he appeared to have been lured to his death for political reasons.

In 2014, Rwanda’s former head of military intelligence, Patrick Karegeya, was found strangled in a hotel room in Johannesburg after he went to meet a friend.

The Rwandan authorities denied both killings, but Mr. Kagame said in a later [interview with The Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702304632204579338811856671086) that he wished that Rwanda had killed Mr. Karegeya.

items.title: SpaceX Swings to a Profit, as A.I. Business Grows
items.summary: Elon Musk’s rocket company said its artificial intelligence spending had soared, but revenue more than doubled from its Starlink internet satellite service and A.I. products.
items.full_text:
Title: SpaceX Swings to a Profit, Even as A.I. Spending Soars - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/technology/spacex-earnings-elon-musk.html

Published Time: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 22:25:53 GMT

Markdown Content:
Since Elon Musk took SpaceX public in June, he has increasingly made the rocket company the center of his business empire.

Mr. Musk recently weighed in on the war in Ukraine when [SpaceX limited its satellite internet service in the country](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/starshield-spacex-ukraine-starlink-satellites-musk.html). He has used hundreds of millions of dollars, fueled partly by his fortune from SpaceX, to [fund Republican groups](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/elon-musk-midterms.html) ahead of the midterm elections. And on Monday, he [pledged one share of SpaceX](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/technology/elon-musk-spacex-stock-anthropic-giveaway.html) to “every kid in America” next year through a government-operated savings account program championed by President Trump.

On Tuesday, SpaceX showed why it continues to be a source of Mr. Musk’s growing influence.

In its second earnings report as a public company, SpaceX said revenue for the three months that ended Sept. 30 was $14.5 billion, more than 2.5 times as much as the $5.6 billion from a year earlier. Profit totaled $4.4 billion, or 37 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $1.05 billion last year.

SpaceX said the results had been driven by its artificial intelligence and satellite internet service businesses. The numbers exceeded the predictions of Wall Street analysts, who had projected revenue of $13 billion and profit of 16 cents a share.

How much SpaceX is spending on A.I. — which includes its Grok chatbot and data centers — was particularly scrutinized. The company said its capital expenditures had risen to $19.6 billion, nearly three times the $6.9 billion from a year earlier. The company did not project its future spending but said its spending on A.I. alone had increased by $4.6 billion since last year, underscoring Mr. Musk’s bet on the rapidly advancing technology.

“We are building the infrastructure of the future with discipline,” SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in a statement.

SpaceX’s stock rose more than 2 percent in after-hours trading. Its shares are trading above their $135 initial public offering price, but have swung up and down.

SpaceX’s performance on the stock market is a barometer for Anthropic, the A.I. company that may go public [as early as next month](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/18/technology/anthropic-ipo-ai-safety.html). OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is also preparing for an initial public offering, which [could come next year](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/25/technology/openai-ipo-artificial-intelligence.html). SpaceX’s results are viewed as offering clues to the direction of the A.I. industry, which has [faced questions](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/business/ai-debt-coreweave-oracle-softbank.html) over whether the spending and borrowing by data center companies such as CoreWeave and Oracle can be sustained.

Melissa Otto, who leads a research group at S&P Global, said she expected SpaceX’s capital expenditures to increase to nearly $195 billion by 2028 from about $70 billion this year. Spending “is what the market is very focused on right now,” she said.

SpaceX’s A.I. spending is supported by its growing connectivity business, which includes its Starlink satellite internet service. The company said it now had 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers, along with hundreds of thousands of enterprise customers.

_This is a developing story. Check back for updates._

Jack Ewing contributed reporting.

items.title: Netflix Is Great at Making Money. Its Problem Is Keeping Viewers Hooked.
items.summary: The streaming service reported a 12 percent increase in quarterly revenue, but acknowledged that stagnant viewership, particularly in the U.S. and Canada, was a major concern.
items.full_text:
Title: Netflix Is Great at Making Money. Its Problem Is Keeping Viewers Hooked. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/business/media/netflix-earnings-ted-sarandos-peter-rice.html

Published Time: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 22:10:14 GMT

Markdown Content:
After a [tumultuous week](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/business/media/netflix-layoffs-bela-bajaria.html), when Netflix laid off 1,000 employees and fired its chief content officer and top two film executives, the world’s largest streaming service showed that one thing isn’t in flux: its ability to make boatloads of money.

The company said on Tuesday that its revenues in the third quarter grew 12 percent from a year earlier, to nearly $12.9 billion, its lowest quarterly revenue percentage growth in three years. Net income rose 44 percent, to nearly $3.7 billion.

For the year, Netflix said, it expects revenue growth to be 13 percent, roughly in line with its previous estimates. Shares dropped about 5 percent in after-hours trading.

The company acknowledged the undercurrent that led to the recent tumult: concern about stagnating attention time on its service.

“We know there’s some investor concern about our view-hours growth,” particularly in the United States and Canada, Netflix told investors in a letter. Revenue in those countries grew 11 percent in the most recent quarter, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Still, the company reiterated that by executing on its strategy for growth — delivering “differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events” while trying to bring “more third-party content to its service” — it will boost engagement time.

Netflix delivered its quarterly results while at a crossroads. Despite being the most-watched paid streaming service in the world, with 325 million subscribers, the company is not growing fast enough for either its top executives or its shareholders.

The time that viewers spend on the service has stagnated, as YouTube increasingly becomes a competitor. Netflix has struggled to create a pipeline of new hits to replace shows like “Stranger Things” and “Squid Game.” Returning shows like “Beef,” “The Night Agent” and “Avatar: The Last Airbender” lost significant viewership for their most recent seasons, according to Netflix’s metrics.

And no film released this summer became a breakout hit, a contrast with last summer, when “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Happy Gilmore 2” captivated viewers. Indeed, the company’s biggest film hit for the quarter was “The Last House,” which generated 91 million views but scored dismally with both critics and audiences.

“Netflix has an engagement problem, and that’s a worrying trend going forward,” wrote Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com. “Users are drifting toward TikTok and YouTube for the attention Netflix used to own, and the trimmed full-year outlook is basically management admitting they can’t see a way back to growth on the current trajectory. Netflix needs another hit on the content side.”

Netflix’s stock has been on a slide since September last year, when it announced its intention to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming business in a nearly $83 billion deal. Even after the company bowed out of the pursuit, not willing to get in a bidding war with the eventual victor, Paramount Skydance, the stock continued to languish. Its price is down nearly 45 percent from a year ago.

Still, last week’s shake-up jolted Hollywood. A day after Netflix announced it was cutting 6 percent of its work force, it fired Bela Bajaria, a well-respected company veteran who, as chief content officer the past three years, expanded Netflix beyond scripted TV shows and movies into reality shows, live events, sports and video podcasts.

Peter Rice, a film and television executive who spent 30 years at Fox before becoming a top executive at Disney, has taken her place.

Beja Bajaria, who had been at Netflix for a decade, and Peter Rice, her successor as chief content officer. Credit...Manoli Figetakis/WireImage, Frank Micelotta/Tubi, via Getty Images

One of his first decisions will be choosing a top film executive to replace [Dan Lin](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/04/business/media/dan-lin-netflix-hollywood.html), who was fired late Friday after two and a half years at the company. Mr. Lin’s mandate to lower production costs and be more selective about what the streaming service makes faced great resistance by the talent. The directors Noah Baumbach and David Fincher ended their relationships with the company.

According to a letter that Mr. Lin sent to his team on his departure, which was obtained by The New York Times, the 53-year-old executive accomplished many of his goals. “For our film slate the past two years, per-title views are up 12 percent and view hours are up 11 percent,” he wrote, adding that in the first half of 2026, 10 of Netflix’s 13 films were rated “loved” by subscribers.

Image

Dan Lin was fired as chairman of Netflix Film last week.Credit...Ahmed Gaber for The New York Times

He leaves behind a robust slate of movies, including “The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” — a sequel of sorts to “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood,” with a script from Quentin Tarantino and directed by Mr. Fincher. It will receive a two-week exclusive IMAX run this year, as will Pete Berg’s war drama, “The Mosquito Bowl.” Next year will bring “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” directed by Greta Gerwig (“Barbie”), and an animated “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory.”

Many in Hollywood are curious whether Mr. Rice will expand Netflix’s tentative foray into releasing films in theaters before they appear on the service. Ted Sarandos, the company’s co-chief executive, has for years insisted that [theatrical distribution is “an outmoded idea,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/05/business/media/netflix-movie-theaters-warner-bros.html) and that Netflix movies are made for its subscribers.

This past weekend, [in a first,](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/business/media/box-office-elizabeth-holmes-netflix.html) the company reported box office grosses for “La Bola Negra,” a Spanish-language multigenerational epic that it acquired at the Cannes Film Festival. The film will remain in theaters for 45 days before it debuts on the service.

Netflix’s television team has also been busy buying up projects over the last year. The streamer gave a straight-to-series order to “The Corrections,” an adaptation of Jonathan Franzen’s 2001 novel, with Meryl Streep expected to star and Cord Jefferson (the writer and director of “American Fiction”) expected to direct the limited series. Netflix also ordered “Rabbit, Rabbit,” a thriller starring Adam Driver and Regina Hall that is expected to premiere next year.

Production also began recently on an adaptation of the Dan Brown novel “The Secret of Secrets.” Carlton Cuse (“Lost,” “Jack Ryan”) is the showrunner, and it stars Morgan Spector (“The Gilded Age”).

The company is banking on these movies and shows, and Mr. Rice’s changes, to reverse the trend of subscribers’ engagement with its offerings. Netflix accounted for 7.8 percent of all television viewing time in the United States in July, according to Nielsen, a full percentage point drop from a year earlier. YouTube’s share was more than 14 percent.

Despite all the turmoil, Netflix maintains a loyal following. According to a report released on Tuesday by Antenna, Netflix has the lowest churn numbers, or cancellation rate, of any streamer.

John Koblin contributed reporting from New York
